1. Meaning and Purpose of a Constitution

  • A Constitution is the fundamental legal framework through which a State is organised and governed.
  • It establishes the principal institutions of government.
  • It defines the powers and limitations of the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary.
  • It regulates relations between different organs of government.
  • It determines how governmental authority is distributed.
  • It provides a framework for the rights and obligations of citizens.
  • It prescribes procedures for making laws and changing the constitutional framework.
  • It provides methods for resolving constitutional disputes.
  • In India, the Constitution is the supreme legal document.
  • Ordinary laws and executive actions must conform to constitutional requirements.
  • A Constitution also provides stable procedures for peaceful political change.
📌 Must-Memorise

Constitution → Creates Institutions + Distributes Power + Limits Power + Protects Rights

2. Functions of a Constitution

  • A Constitution creates institutions through which public power is exercised.
  • It determines which authority can make laws, implement laws and interpret laws.
  • It distributes powers between different levels of government.
  • It restricts arbitrary governmental action.
  • It protects individuals and communities.
  • It establishes procedures for formation and change of governments.
  • It provides mechanisms for resolving institutional disputes.
  • It establishes methods for constitutional amendment.
  • It permits political change without requiring destruction of the constitutional State.

3. Constitution and Constitutionalism

  • A Constitution establishes the structure and powers of government.
  • Constitutionalism means that those powers are genuinely limited and exercised according to constitutional principles.
  • A State may possess a written Constitution but may fail to practise constitutionalism.
  • Constitutionalism requires limited government.
  • It requires Rule of Law.
  • It requires governmental accountability.
  • It requires protection of rights.
  • It requires institutional distribution of powers.
  • It requires independent adjudication.
  • It requires government to operate through legally prescribed procedures.
  • A Constitution without constitutionalism may remain only a formal legal document.
📌 Must-Memorise

Constitution → Establishes Government

Constitutionalism → Limits Government

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Constitution ≠ Constitutionalism

4. Limited Government and Constitutional Supremacy

  • Limited government does not mean weak government.
  • It means that governmental powers are legally defined and constitutionally controlled.
  • Public authorities must exercise power under constitutional authority.
  • Constitutional procedures must be followed.
  • Rulers themselves are subject to law.
  • Citizens possess constitutional protections against arbitrary State action.
  • In India, Parliament, the Executive and other governmental institutions derive their authority from the Constitution.
  • No ordinary organ of government possesses unlimited constitutional power.
  • India therefore follows constitutional supremacy.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Constitutional Supremacy

5. Regulating Act, 1773

  • The Regulating Act, 1773 was the first major attempt by the British Parliament to regulate East India Company administration in India.
  • It marked the beginning of increased parliamentary control over Company rule.
  • The Governor of Bengal was redesignated as the Governor-General of Bengal.
  • Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General of Bengal.
  • The Governor-General was assisted by an Executive Council of four members.
  • The Presidencies of Bombay and Madras were made subordinate to Bengal in important matters.
  • The Act provided for establishment of a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
  • The Supreme Court at Calcutta began functioning in 1774.

Regulating Act 1773 → Warren Hastings → First Governor-General of Bengal

Supreme Court at Calcutta → 1774

6. Pitt's India Act, 1784

  • Pitt's India Act, 1784 strengthened British governmental supervision over East India Company administration.
  • It created the Board of Control.
  • The Court of Directors continued to handle mainly the Company's commercial affairs.
  • The Board of Control supervised political and administrative matters.
  • This arrangement is commonly described as dual control.
  • The Act further distinguished the Company's commercial functions from its political functions.

7. Charter Act, 1813

  • The Charter Act, 1813 substantially ended the East India Company's monopoly over trade with India.
  • The Company retained its monopoly over tea trade and trade with China for the time being.
  • The Act permitted Christian missionaries to operate more freely in British India.
  • It provided an annual sum of ₹1 lakh for the promotion of education.
  • It further asserted British parliamentary authority over Company administration.

8. Charter Act, 1833

  • The Charter Act, 1833 made major administrative changes in British India.
  • It redesignated the Governor-General of Bengal as the Governor-General of India.
  • Lord William Bentinck became the first Governor-General of India.
  • Legislative authority was significantly centralised.
  • The Governors of Bombay and Madras lost their independent legislative powers.
  • The East India Company's remaining commercial activities were terminated.
  • The Company thereafter functioned principally as an administrative agency.
  • The Act provided for establishment of a Law Commission.
  • The First Law Commission was constituted in 1834.
  • Lord Macaulay became Chairman of the First Law Commission.

9. Charter Act, 1853

  • The Charter Act, 1853 was the last Charter Act relating to the East India Company.
  • It more clearly separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council.
  • Additional members were included for legislative purposes.
  • It opened the way towards recruitment to the civil services through competition.
  • The Macaulay Committee of 1854 subsequently recommended a competitive system for civil-service recruitment.

  • The Government of India Act, 1858 ended East India Company rule.
  • Administration of India was transferred directly to the British Crown.
  • The Court of Directors and Board of Control were abolished.
  • The office of Secretary of State for India was created.
  • The Secretary of State was assisted by a Council of India.
  • The Governor-General also became known as the Viceroy as representative of the British Crown.
  • Lord Canning became the first Viceroy of India.

11. Indian Councils Act, 1861

  • The Indian Councils Act, 1861 expanded legislative councils.
  • Indians could be nominated to the Governor-General's Legislative Council for legislative work.
  • Lord Canning nominated Indians to the Council.
  • Legislative powers were restored to Bombay and Madras.
  • The Act therefore initiated limited legislative decentralisation.
  • The portfolio system of administration developed during this period.

12. Indian Councils Act, 1892

  • The Indian Councils Act, 1892 increased the number of members in central and provincial legislative councils.
  • It introduced an indirect electoral element.
  • The word "election" was not formally used in the Act.
  • Members were allowed to discuss the annual budget.
  • Members could ask questions subject to prescribed conditions.
  • The Act expanded participation without establishing responsible government.

13. Indian Councils Act, 1909 — Morley–Minto Reforms

  • The Indian Councils Act, 1909 is popularly known as the Morley–Minto Reforms.
  • John Morley was the Secretary of State for India.
  • Lord Minto was the Viceroy.
  • Membership of central and provincial legislative councils was increased.
  • The elective principle was expanded.
  • Separate electorates were introduced for Muslims.
  • Muslim voters elected Muslim representatives under the separate-electorate arrangement.
  • This formally institutionalised communal political representation.
  • Satyendra Prasanna Sinha became the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council.
  • He served as Law Member.

14. Government of India Act, 1919 — Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms

  • The Government of India Act, 1919 implemented the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms.
  • It introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
  • Provincial subjects were divided into Reserved Subjects and Transferred Subjects.
  • Reserved Subjects were administered by the Governor and Executive Council.
  • Transferred Subjects were administered by ministers responsible to the provincial legislature.
  • Bicameralism was introduced at the Centre.
  • The two central Houses were the Council of State and Legislative Assembly.
  • Direct elections were introduced on a restricted franchise.
  • Communal representation was extended.
  • Central and provincial budgets were separated.
  • The Act provided for establishment of a Public Service Commission.
  • India's first Public Service Commission was established in 1926.
📌 Must-Memorise

1919 Act → Bicameralism at Centre

18. Government of India Act, 1935

  • The Government of India Act, 1935 was the most extensive British constitutional statute relating to India.
  • It became the largest single administrative source used by the Constitution-makers.
  • It proposed an All-India Federation consisting of British Indian provinces and princely states.
  • The proposed federation never fully came into operation.
  • Provincial autonomy was introduced.
  • Dyarchy in the provinces was abolished.
  • Dyarchy was proposed at the Centre but never became operational.
  • Legislative subjects were divided into the Federal List, Provincial List and Concurrent List.
  • Residuary powers were vested in the Governor-General.
  • Bicameral legislatures were provided in certain provinces.
  • Separate electorates and communal representation continued.
  • The Act provided for establishment of a Federal Court.
  • The Federal Court of India began functioning in 1937.
  • It also provided for Public Service Commissions.
  • Provisions relating to Governors, public services, federal relations, legislative lists, administration and emergencies later influenced the Constitution of India.

1935 Act → Federal + Provincial + Concurrent Lists

Federal Court → 1937

19. Indian Independence Act, 1947

  • The Indian Independence Act was enacted by the British Parliament in July 1947.
  • It created the two independent Dominions of India and Pakistan.
  • British rule ended on 15 August 1947.
  • British parliamentary authority over the new Dominions ceased.
  • British paramountcy over princely states lapsed.
  • The office of Secretary of State for India was abolished.
  • The Constituent Assemblies of India and Pakistan received legislative and constitution-making authority.
  • Until their own Constitutions came into force, administration continued largely under the Government of India Act, 1935 as adapted.

20. Demand for a Constituent Assembly

  • Indian constitutional demands gradually shifted from colonial reforms towards the principle that Indians themselves must frame their Constitution.
  • M.N. Roy is commonly credited with advancing the idea of a Constituent Assembly in 1934.
  • The Indian National Congress subsequently adopted the demand.
  • In 1938, Jawaharlal Nehru declared that the Constitution of free India should be framed by a Constituent Assembly elected on the basis of adult franchise without external interference.
  • The August Offer, 1940 accepted in principle that Indians would participate in framing a new constitutional order after World War II.
  • The Cripps Mission, 1942 proposed a post-war constitution-making body.
  • Major Indian political forces rejected the Cripps proposals as inadequate.
  • The Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946 finally provided the practical framework for formation of the Constituent Assembly.
📌 Must-Memorise

Constituent Assembly Idea → M.N. Roy → 1934

Practical Constituent Assembly Scheme → Cabinet Mission → 1946

21. Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946

  • The Cabinet Mission came to India in 1946.
  • Its three members were Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander.
  • The Mission provided the practical scheme for creation of the Constituent Assembly.
  • Representation was broadly based on population.
  • Approximately one seat was allotted for every one million persons.
  • Representatives of British Indian provinces were indirectly elected by Provincial Legislative Assemblies.
  • Election was conducted through proportional representation using the single transferable vote.
  • Provincial seats were distributed broadly among General, Muslim and Sikh categories.
  • Representatives of princely states were to be nominated by their rulers or selected through arrangements within those States.
  • Universal adult franchise was not used for the Constituent Assembly election.
  • The Muslim League initially boycotted the Assembly.
  • Partition later changed the membership and territorial representation of the Assembly.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cabinet Mission → Pethick-Lawrence + Cripps + A.V. Alexander

Constituent Assembly Election → Proportional Representation + Single Transferable Vote

Not Directly Elected through Universal Adult Franchise

22. Original Composition of the Constituent Assembly

  • The original strength of the Constituent Assembly was 389.
  • Governors' Provinces were allotted 292 seats.
  • Chief Commissioners' Provinces were allotted 4 seats.
  • Princely states were allotted 93 seats.
  • Thus, 292 + 4 + 93 = 389.
  • Congress emerged as the dominant political group.
  • The Assembly included national leaders, lawyers, administrators, social reformers, minority representatives, tribal representatives and women.
  • It also contained representatives of Scheduled Castes, Anglo-Indians, Parsis, Christians and Sikhs.
  • The Assembly was criticised because it was indirectly elected and universal adult franchise had not been used.
  • Princely-state representatives were not uniformly elected.
  • The Muslim League's boycott also affected its early representative character.

389 = 292 + 4 + 93

23. Constituent Assembly after Partition

  • Partition fundamentally changed the composition of the Assembly.
  • Representatives belonging to territories that became Pakistan left the Indian Constituent Assembly.
  • Membership was reduced from 389 to 299.
  • Of the 299 members, 229 represented provinces.
  • The remaining 70 represented princely states.
  • After independence, the Constituent Assembly became a sovereign constitution-making body.
  • It also performed legislative functions for the Dominion of India.

39. Role of B.R. Ambedkar

  • Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.
  • He introduced the Draft Constitution before the Constituent Assembly.
  • He explained and defended constitutional provisions during detailed debates.
  • He responded to numerous proposed amendments.
  • He emphasised constitutional remedies.
  • He stressed both political democracy and social democracy.
  • He supported constitutional safeguards for historically disadvantaged groups.
  • He warned against abandoning constitutional methods after independence.
  • He is widely referred to as the Chief Architect or Father of the Indian Constitution because of his central role.
  • These descriptions do not mean that he alone wrote the Constitution.
  • Constitution-making was a collective institutional process involving the full Assembly, committees, advisers, draftsmen and public suggestions.

42. Preparation of the Draft Constitution

  • The Assembly's committees first examined subjects including Union structure, provincial constitutions, Fundamental Rights, minorities, tribal areas and distribution of powers.
  • B.N. Rau prepared a preliminary draft using committee reports, comparative constitutional research, existing Indian laws and Assembly decisions.
  • The Drafting Committee received Rau's draft and scrutinised, modified and expanded it.
  • The Drafting Committee submitted its Draft Constitution to the President of the Constituent Assembly on 21 February 1948.
  • The 1948 Draft contained 315 Articles, 18 Parts and 8 Schedules.
  • It was widely circulated to Assembly members, governments, ministries, courts and the public for comments.
  • During 1948, the Drafting Committee reconsidered the Draft in light of suggestions received.
  • A revised set of proposals was prepared before formal Assembly consideration.
  • B.R. Ambedkar introduced the Draft Constitution in the Assembly on 4 November 1948. (Constitution of India)

43. Three Readings of the Draft Constitution

  • The First Reading began with Ambedkar's introduction on 4 November 1948.
  • General discussion continued until 9 November 1948.
  • The Second Reading began on 15 November 1948.
  • During the Second Reading, the Assembly considered the Draft article by article.

63. Need for Constitutional Amendment

  • A Constitution must provide stability while also permitting peaceful change.
  • Constitutional amendments may become necessary because of social change.
  • They may respond to administrative requirements.
  • They may introduce institutional reforms.
  • They may respond to judicial interpretations.
  • They may alter federal arrangements.
  • They may expand democratic participation.
  • The Indian Constitution therefore combines continuity with adaptability.

64. Article 368

  • Article 368 deals with Parliament's constituent power and procedure for constitutional amendment.
  • Not every change affecting the Constitution is technically made under Article 368.
  • The Constitution broadly permits three methods of change.
  • Some provisions may be changed by simple majority.
  • Most constitutional amendments require a special majority of Parliament.
  • Specified federal amendments require a special parliamentary majority plus ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 368 → Constitutional Amendment

65. Amendment by Simple Majority

  • Certain constitutional matters may be altered by an ordinary legislative majority.
  • Such changes are technically outside the Article 368 amendment procedure.
  • Examples include specified matters relating to formation and alteration of States.
  • Creation or abolition of State Legislative Councils may also be dealt with through the special constitutional procedure involving ordinary parliamentary legislation.
  • Certain citizenship-related and procedural matters may also be changed by ordinary legislation.
  • Such provisions demonstrate the flexible aspect of the Constitution.

66. Amendment by Special Majority

  • Most constitutional amendments require a special majority in each House of Parliament.
  • The Bill must be supported by a majority of the total membership of the House.
  • It must also receive the support of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
  • Both conditions must be satisfied.
  • Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha must separately pass the amendment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Special Majority → Total Membership Majority + Two-Thirds Present and Voting

67. Amendments Requiring State Ratification

  • Specified amendments affecting India's federal structure require ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures.
  • These include amendments affecting the election of the President.
  • They include specified provisions concerning Union and State executive powers.
  • They include the Supreme Court and High Courts.
  • They include the distribution of legislative powers.
  • They include the Seventh Schedule.
  • They include representation of States in Parliament.
  • They include Article 368 itself.
  • Ratification by all States is not required.
📌 Must-Memorise

68. Constitutional Amendment Bill

  • A Constitution Amendment Bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament.
  • A State Legislature cannot initiate a Constitution Amendment Bill.
  • Each House must pass it separately.
  • There is no provision for a joint sitting to resolve disagreement between the two Houses.
  • States ratify only those amendments for which State ratification is constitutionally required.
  • No fixed constitutional time limit is prescribed for State ratification.
  • After the required procedure is completed, the Bill is presented to the President.
  • The President must give assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill duly passed under Article 368.

69. Amendment Power and Basic Structure

  • Parliament's amending power is extensive but not unlimited.
  • The Supreme Court developed limitations on constitutional amendment through judicial decisions.
  • In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973, the Supreme Court held that Parliament may amend the Constitution but cannot destroy its Basic Structure.
  • The Basic Structure Doctrine therefore protects the essential constitutional identity of India.

70. Constitutional Supremacy and Importance

  • All governmental institutions derive their authority from the Constitution.
  • Legislative actions must conform to constitutional limitations.
  • Executive power must be exercised under constitutional authority.
  • Courts enforce constitutional limitations through judicial processes.
  • The Constitution establishes democratic legitimacy through representative institutions.
  • It provides for periodic elections and adult franchise.
  • It establishes mechanisms of political accountability.
  • It accommodates India's regional, linguistic, religious and social diversity.
  • It establishes peaceful methods for political competition and institutional change.
  • It therefore operates simultaneously as a legal, political and social document.

71. Constitution and Social Transformation

  • The Constitution does more than organise governmental institutions.
  • It seeks to transform Indian society through equality and social justice.
  • It provides a constitutional framework against discriminatory practices.
  • It protects disadvantaged groups.
  • It promotes democratic participation.
  • It creates a framework for welfare-oriented governance.
  • It seeks to combine political democracy with social and economic transformation.

72. Constitution as a Living Document

  • The Constitution combines legal continuity with capacity for change.
  • It evolves through formal constitutional amendments.
  • Judicial interpretation develops constitutional meaning.
  • Legislative action affects the operation of constitutional provisions.
  • Constitutional conventions influence governmental practice.
  • Institutional practices shape constitutional functioning.
  • Democratic participation also influences constitutional development.
  • This capacity to adapt while preserving constitutional continuity is why the Constitution is often described as a living document.
